P01.passage: In 1838 a merchant inherited an estate of farms and oak woods worked by hired hands, and his account books for the next twenty years survive. In 1840 they record three sums, from a neighboring landowner, a timber merchant and an auctioneer, together larger than thirty years of the estate's profits. After that come no wages, rents or repairs at all, only half-yearly dividends from railway shares. From those books, one historian concluded that, above all, he had ______ the estate.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: In 1952 a museum sent a sixteenth-century altarpiece, painted on three oak panels and darkened by four centuries of candle smoke and varnish, to a restoration workshop for two years. The oak had shrunk and split along its grain, lifting the paint into blisters that flaked away whenever the church's heating came on. The restorers spent two years laying each blister back down with warm wax and setting the panels in a frame that let the wood move, and they returned the altarpiece as dark with smoke and varnish as it had arrived. Reviewing the work in 1960, one curator wrote that the restorers had, above all, ______ the altarpiece.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: A canal dug in the 1300s runs for two miles beside the old center of a river city, along the line of a wall the city had already outgrown and pulled down. Its water comes from springs in the hills, while the city's wells, sunk in marsh ground near the river, draw water too brackish to drink. Watchmen kept barges, laundry and loiterers off it, and wooden pipes carried its water to fountains in the quarters on both its banks. In her history of the city, one historian called the canal, above all, the city's ______.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: From 1950 to 1990, scientists studied one small, deep, cold lake in a northern forest more closely than any other lake in the region, and its bottom mud lies in fine yearly layers. In its cold depths live a shrimp and a small fish that vanished from every other lake in the region as the ice age ended, and scientists came to it to study what the region's lakes had held then. Burrowing worms have churned its layers past reading. In a history of that work, one scientist called the lake, for those four decades, above all the region's ______.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: In 1883 a volcano erupted on a small island off a mountainous coast, where a fishing village had stood above a sheltered harbor for three centuries, with farms on the slopes behind it. Sailing in twenty years later, surveyors found the harbor's breakwater far below the surface, and every benchmark cut on the island in 1880 sat nine meters lower than the old chart showed. Fishermen dropped anchor above the village's walls, which still stood, and the farms on the upper slopes were planted as before. Revisiting the island in 1903, one geologist wrote that the eruption had ______ it.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: In 1987 a plowman near an old river landing turned up a clay pot buried around the year 900, holding some nine hundred silver coins and pieces of cut silver. Most of the silver is scrap: brooches and arm rings cut into pieces, small bars cast from melted pieces, and a set of balance weights, and many coins are nicked with a knife to test their metal. The pot lay in the floor of a workshop with a small furnace and crucibles. From its contents, one archaeologist concluded that the hoard had been, above all, its owners' ______.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: A potter fired a batch of white bowls painted with blue brushwork under a clear glaze. The kiln had been heated twice as fast as usual. A fingertip drawn across any bowl caught on hundreds of tiny raised rims, each around a pinhole, and the brushwork showed between them as clearly as before. A week later the bowls had held tea without a mark. In her notes on the batch, the potter concluded that the firing had ______ the glaze.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: In 1958 an expressway was built up a river valley, joining a mill town of eight thousand people to a growing city twenty miles south. The road followed the riverbank below the town, on land the railroad had abandoned. Within a decade the farms along it had been sold for houses, and by 1990 a driver from the city passed no open field on the way. The town then had twenty-six thousand people, its mill held a city insurer's offices, and most stores on its main street were branches of city chains. In a 1990 study, one planner argued that the expressway had, above all, ______ the town.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: A rocky island of two square miles, with a stone quay and a row of warehouses, lies in a strait between the ocean and an inland sea lined with port cities. The strait's only deep channel runs beneath the island's cliffs, among shoals that no outside captain knew. Every inbound ship tied up at the quay while customs clerks from the cities opened its cargo in the warehouses, and that same day an island pilot steered it, fully reloaded, the forty miles to the cities. One historian has argued that through the nineteenth century the island served those cities above all as their ______.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: From 1850 to 1950 a small country taxed every bushel of wheat brought in through its ports, and the rate changed eleven times. Each change came in a year when wheat prices had slumped and farm members of parliament pressed for help, and each one raised the rate. In the good years that followed, bills to lower it always failed, and by 1950 the duty stood at nine times its first level. The neighboring countries had raised their own grain duties years before it did. Surveying that century, one economist calls the duty a kind of ______.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: In a pond where half the snails carry a parasitic worm that matures inside ducks, a biologist kept infected and uninfected snails side by side for three years, in tanks and in a pen with feeding ducks. Infected snails grew as large, laid as many eggs and lived as long as the others in the tanks. In the pen they climbed to the sunlit tips of the weeds at midday, where ducks feed, while uninfected snails stayed low in the shade, and a bacterium that swept the tanks killed both kinds alike. From these results, she concluded that the worm had, above all, ______ its host.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: A cave high in a cliff overlooks a ford where reindeer herds crossed a river each spring and autumn fourteen thousand years ago; its back chamber stays near freezing all year. In that chamber excavators found reindeer leg bones stacked in piles, most still joined at the knee and none burned, while the hearths, tools and children's teeth of the period lay in a camp by the river. Bones in the camp's late-winter hearths were the same cuts from the autumn herds, cracked open for marrow. From the finds, one archaeologist concluded that the valley's hunters used the cave above all as their ______.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: A chalk quarry worked out in the 1800s lies at the edge of a market town, a pit two hundred yards across with galleries cut back into its walls. Since 1870 the gutters of the town's lower streets have run downhill into it, carrying whatever the streets carry. Its floor is a black pond whose smell reaches the market square on still summer days, and no one has fished or skated on it in living memory. Its galleries are flooded to their roofs. One local historian has called the quarry, above all, the town's ______.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: In 1894 a court ruled on a strike by a port city's dockworkers' union, which then had four thousand members and a hall near the docks. The court held that the skilled crane operators could lawfully strike and the laborers could not strike in their support. Within a year the operators had formed their own association, and in 1902 its members crossed a laborers' picket line around the docks; the laborers, still in the old union, won that strike after nine weeks. Both bodies still bargained there in 1944. Writing fifty years later, one labor historian concluded that the ruling had, in effect, ______ the union.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: Each winter ice covers much of a northern bay where seals, seabirds, cod, and krill live. The ice there breaks into floes that drift south with the current. Late in winter harp seals climb onto the floes to give birth, and the pups lie there nursing for two weeks before they can swim. By then the floes are a hundred miles south, near the shoals where young seals feed. The floes are thick and snow-covered, and almost nothing grows beneath them. One marine biologist has written that the bay's winter ice serves its animals above all as their ______.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: Astronomers modeled a young planetary system with small rocky planets near its star, a belt of icy bodies far out, and a giant planet between them, running the model once with the giant and once without it. With the giant present, a swarm of icy bodies gathered in the giant's own orbit, a sixth of a circuit ahead of it, and stayed there for the whole billion years, moving in step with the giant. The belt itself spread and thinned much as it did without the giant, and the rocky planets were struck about equally often in both runs. One astronomer described the giant as, above all, the system's ______.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: In 1931 a port city required every fishing boat landing there to sell its whole catch at a single dawn auction on the quay; before, each crew had sold to any buyer it chose, whenever it chose. A fishing village four miles down the coast, where crews could still sell to any buyer at any hour, built a new quay in 1932. By 1936 most of the city's boats and nearly all of its fish buyers did their business there, and the fleet working the coast had grown by a third. Writing in 1960, one economist argued that the rule had ______ the city's fish market.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: For five years of wartime occupation, a city's public library of some three hundred thousand volumes was under the control of the occupying authority. When the staff returned, most shelves stood full and the rare-book room was untouched; every book by some two hundred writers, most of them critics of the occupiers, had gone, along with those writers' catalog cards. A police log records a bonfire of books in the square outside in 1941. In a postwar report, one librarian concluded that the occupation had ______ the library.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: A great stone temple was finished in a river city in 1580; a smaller wooden temple stands on a hill a day's walk north. A lord of the northern hills built it, and its monks came from a coastal order with no tie to the city temple's. He set its festival for the same spring week as the city's, beneath a gate carved taller than the city temple's. Within ten years the city's festival tolls had fallen by half. One architectural historian concludes that the hill temple is best understood as the city temple's ______.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: In 1904 a new firm began making typewriters in a country where one older company had sold nearly every machine for thirty years, and by 1914 the newcomer was outselling it. Its first machine matched the older company's model part for part, down to the shape of the keys. Its engineers had bought that model in shops and taken it apart, and the newcomer sold its version through the same dealers as the older firm, at a lower price. Reading both firms' records, one historian concluded that the newcomer had above all ______ its rival.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: A cave opens in the side of a limestone hill above a village, and its passages wind back for a mile under the hill. A second, smaller opening breaks the surface near the hilltop. Through the winter a steady draft enters at the lower mouth and leaves at the upper one, where a plume of vapor stands over the hill on frosty mornings. The drips from the cave's roof gather into a brook that runs out of the lower mouth. In a survey of the district, one geologist called the cave, above all, the hill's ______.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: In 1897 gold was found in the hills above a small river town, and the rush lasted six years. The diggings lay a day's ride away, and in the first summer the farmhands left for them, flour tripled in price, and farmers borrowed against their land to match the miners' wages. When the gold gave out in 1903 the bank called in its loans, and half the farms went to auction. By 1920 the town had four hundred people where it had had eight hundred, its main street still facing the river landing. Looking back in 1920, one historian wrote that the gold rush had ______ the town.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: A sand spit four miles long curves across a lagoon's mouth, with a lighthouse near its hooked tip and a road along its crest. In 1953 a three-day gale drove waves over the crest. Afterward the reeds on the lagoon side lay under two feet of beach sand, and boathouses that had stood at the water's edge stood two hundred yards from it. The next week the keeper drove the road past the lighthouse to the hooked tip. All spring the wind lifted the new sand off the lagoon side. Comparing surveys made before and after that winter, one geologist concluded that the gale had ______ the spit.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: In 1965 a carmaker from abroad opened a plant outside a port city, on a site its board had chosen after two years of study. Built of glass on the highway from the airport, it ran tours for ministers and newspaper editors every week and assembled thirty cars a month, most of them lent to officials, with forty workers flown in from the head office. The company never built another plant in the country, and for decades its imported cars sold through dealers who pointed buyers to the glass building. In a history of the company, one economist called the plant, above all, its ______ in the country.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: A rocky island a quarter mile long lies in the middle of a wide river where it crosses a farming valley. Gravel shallows run out to it from both banks, and in late summer the valley's harvest carts reach the market town on the far bank by way of the island. Along both its shores the current runs too fast for a barge to tie up. Raiders coming downriver in 1640 burned the island's barns with the valley's, and the spring floods cover it. In a history of the valley, one historian called the island, above all, the valley's ______.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: A mountain river flows through a narrow lake and then forty miles down to a valley, whose canals feed orchards and trout ponds that fail when the water passes seventy degrees. Springs across the lake's broad, flat floor feed it the year round, and its outflow runs a third larger than its inflow, in drought years as in wet ones. Spread thin over that floor, the water leaves as icy in January and as warm in August as the river arrives, so the ponds are stocked only in spring and fall. One hydrologist has described the lake as serving the river as a kind of ______.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: Between the two world wars, exiles working for their small homeland's independence gathered at a café in a foreign capital, where the owner kept the back room for them. The movement's committee sat in another country, and the capital's reporters who came asking for the exiles' case were handed its address. Each week the old poet at the long table set the newest arrivals from home an essay on the homeland's history and the next night took it apart before them all. Within ten years those students edited all the movement's papers. In a memoir of those years, one journalist called the café, more than anything, the movement's ______.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: Between 1925 and 1935 a record company sent engineers into a mountain region to record its fiddlers and ballad singers, and it sold the records by the thousand. A record side held three minutes, so singers cut twenty-verse ballads to five or six verses for the microphone, and the region's young people, learning the songs from the records, sang only those verses. The singers' rough voices and odd fiddle tunings went onto the records as the engineers had found them, and porches and dances across the region rang with the songs for decades. Looking back in 1970, one folklorist argued that the records had ______ the region's songs.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: In 1921 a state agricultural college opened a station on forty acres in a wheat-growing district of the plains, two years after drought had closed the district's last seed merchant. That spring its staff sowed all forty acres, watered from the college's deep well, with the district's usual wheat and sold the harvest to farmers as seed at cost, one wagonload per farm. A seed company opened a store in the county seat in 1925, and the next spring the college turned the station's fields over to cattle. In a history of farming on the plains, one economist describes the station as, above all, the district's ______.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: In 1952, after three dry years, a river broke its banks and spread for five days across a broad valley, filling every side channel between its villages and their fields. It came down brown from eroding hill country and, as it drained, left a skin of dark mud over every field it had covered. The water soaked away within weeks, and that winter the wheat on the flooded farms withered as badly as on the dry terraces above; the next three harvests, in years of ordinary rain, were the largest the valley had recorded. One agronomist later argued that, for the farmers, the flood had above all ______ their fields.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: In 1980 a storm dropped a two-hundred-year-old fir into a mountain stream, and its trunk, four feet thick, has lain there ever since. It came to rest high across the stream, its ends on the two banks, above every flood since. Its bark has rotted into a soft bed, and hemlock and huckleberry seedlings, which rarely take hold in the thick moss of the forest floor, now stand in a dense row along its whole length, some already taller than a man. After a decade of watching it, one ecologist called the log, above all, the valley's ______.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: For eighty years after 1890, companies mined copper from a mountain above a valley town, until the last mine closed in 1972. The ore came up a single shaft from one deep vein, and from the town the slopes and the summit cairn of 1885 look as they do in old photographs. Water seeping from the old workings runs orange down every stream on the mountain, the trout that once rose in them are gone, and along the streambanks the forest has died back to bare gray trunks. Surveying the mountain in 1980, one geologist wrote that mining had ______ it.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: In 1976 almost no rain fell for eleven summer weeks on a trout river that runs twenty miles from upland springs to a lake. By the eighth week the flow at the gauge halfway down had fallen to a fifth of its usual summer level, and it never stopped. Anglers could step across the river at any riffle, between wide margins of dry white gravel, and trout moved freely up and down it from bend to bend. Nearly all of them were alive when the autumn rains came. In a report on that summer, one hydrologist wrote that the drought had ______ the river.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: In 1590 the council of a river city built a stone granary on its market square, large enough to hold a year's grain for every household. Its stock was renewed each autumn and otherwise left untouched, while merchants supplied the city's bread at prices that rose and fell with each harvest. In 1630, 1698 and 1740 the harvest failed across the province, and in each of those years the council opened its doors in late winter, selling to every household at the previous year's price. One economic historian has argued that for two centuries the granary served above all as the city's ______.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: In 1650 a printed collection brought to a mountain region a long tale, set in a distant desert capital, of a merchant's son who outwits a robber king. The printed tale ran to forty pages and eleven episodes. The village versions recorded around 1900 took about three minutes to tell and kept a single episode, the robber king's riddle and the son's answer, in nearly the words of the 1650 text and still set in the desert capital. In a 1905 study, one folklorist argued that centuries of village retelling had, above all, ______ the tale.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: A gravel bar a mile long runs from the southern shore of a bay toward an island at the bay's mouth. Between its end and the island runs a gut sixty yards wide, deep enough for a keel at any tide, and reefs fill the water beyond the island. At high water only a few feet covers the rest of the crest, and winter swells roll across it into the bay. Since 1650 a harbor boat moored in the gut has collected the town's dues. One historian of the bay's fishing town wrote that the bar had served the town above all as its ______.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: A single hawthorn hedge runs a mile east to west across open plowed fields between two oak woods, and voles burrow thickly in the bank beneath it. Each autumn young stoats leave the eastern wood to find territories, and nearly every adult trapped in the western wood had been collared as a kit in the east. Collared young entered the hedge at dusk and came out of its western end within an hour, and in six years a stoat was seen in the open fields only twice. After six years of tracking collared stoats there, one ecologist concluded that the animals used the hedge above all as their ______.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: For six centuries an oasis of palms and wells stood alone on the caravan road across a desert, eleven days from the river and nine from the coast. For eleven months its wells served only a few families who grew their own dates. Each spring, when the rains brought grass, herders from every part of the desert and caravans from both ends of the road met there for a month of trading, racing and weddings, and then scattered back the way they had come. In a history of the road, one scholar described the oasis as, above all, the desert's ______.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: In the spring of 1952 a river in a dry farming valley flooded the lower fields, where irrigation had left a pale crust of salt. The water came down from the upland meadows, ran off the hard crust within a day, and left last year's stubble standing. Next spring the fallow fields came up thick with wild rye and bluestem, grasses the valley had only on those meadows. On the sown ones, the same seed wheat yielded half as much as on the upper slopes, as it always had. In a report on the valley's farms, one soil scientist wrote that the flood had ______ the lower fields.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: In 1925 each large city in one country had its own daily newspaper, and the papers jointly owned the wire service that supplied their national news. Radio stations offered to pay for the wire service's bulletins. Papers in the larger cities voted to sell; the rest refused, fearing listeners would stop buying papers. In 1934 the larger papers began taking their national news from a new service that the stations helped fund. The stations had no reporters and read its bulletins only after the morning papers were out, and both groups' circulation kept rising. Writing in 1960, one press historian concluded that radio had ______ the country's newspapers.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
